title: THE BLOOD OF JESUS CLEANSES US FROM ALL SIN… BUT HAVE YOU READ WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS RIGHT BEFORE THAT PROMISE?
paragraphs: THE BLOOD OF JESUS CLEANSES US FROM ALL SIN… BUT HAVE YOU READ WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS RIGHT BEFORE THAT PROMISE?
The terrifying danger of hiding in darkness, the beautiful truth about walking in the light, and the grace of Jesus Christ that can reach even the parts of your life you are ashamed to reveal.
There is a Bible verse that millions of Christians love to quote.
It has comforted the guilty. Given hope to the broken. Brought tears to people who thought they had gone too far to be forgiven.
“The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7 (KJV)
What a promise.
ALL sin.
Not just the respectable sins.
Not just the mistakes you can explain away.
Not just the things you did before you became a Christian.
All sin.
But there is something in that verse that we cannot afford to ignore.
Something written before those beautiful words about the blood of Jesus.
Something that should make every person who calls themselves a follower of Christ stop, examine their heart, and ask a question they may have been avoiding for years.
Because the apostle John did not simply write, “The blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.”
He wrote:
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7 (KJV)
But if we walk in the light…
Did you catch that?
John connects walking in the light with fellowship and the cleansing blood of Jesus.
And suddenly, this familiar verse becomes more than a comforting sentence we post on social media.
It becomes an invitation to examine how we are actually living.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to forgive sinners.
Not because we must somehow become perfect before His blood can cleanse us.
But because the same Gospel that offers forgiveness also calls us out of darkness.
And there is a difference between struggling with sin while coming honestly to Jesus and making peace with sin while claiming to belong to Him.
That difference matters.
More than many of us realize.
Imagine someone sitting alone in a dark bedroom at two in the morning.
The house is quiet.
Their family thinks they are asleep.
Their friends think they are doing well.
Their church knows them as someone who loves God.
They post Bible verses. They say amen. They encourage other people to pray.
But there is another part of their life nobody sees.
The secret messages.
The hidden habits.
The bitterness they keep feeding.
The pornography they keep returning to.
The lies they have learned to tell so naturally that even they are beginning to believe them.
Or perhaps their struggle is not something scandalous by human standards.
Perhaps it is envy.
Pride.
A heart that cannot forgive.
A private hunger for approval.
A religious appearance covering a soul that has grown cold toward God.
They know something is wrong.
They have prayed about it before.
They have promised to stop.
They have cried.
They have failed.
And now, somewhere between exhaustion and shame, they whisper something terrifying:
“Maybe this is just who I am.”
But what if that is not the end of their story?
What if the very thing they are desperately trying to hide is the thing they need to bring into the light of Christ?
And what if the blood of Jesus is not an excuse to remain in darkness, but the reason a sinner can finally stop hiding?
That is where John's message begins to become painfully personal.
The apostle writes:
Notice what John does not say.
He does not merely say that God possesses light.
He says God is light.
His holiness is not something He occasionally displays.
His purity is not something He switches on when people are watching.
There is no moral darkness in Him.
No corruption.
No deception.
No hidden wickedness.
No contradiction between what He says and who He is.
And because God is light, fellowship with Him cannot be built upon a deliberate love of darkness.
John continues:
“If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth.” — 1 John 1:6 (KJV)
Those words are uncomfortable.
Especially in a generation where it is possible to look spiritually alive in public while slowly dying inside.
John is not describing a believer who has stumbled, grieved over sin, and returned to Christ in repentance.
He is confronting the contradiction of claiming fellowship with God while living in darkness.
A profession of faith cannot make deliberate rebellion holy.
A Christian label cannot transform dishonesty into truth.
Religious activity cannot substitute for genuine fellowship with Jesus.
You can know the language of worship without surrendering your heart.
You can recognize every familiar Bible verse while refusing to obey the One who inspired Scripture.
You can appear close to God in the eyes of people while resisting His correction in secret.
And perhaps the most dangerous part is how normal it can begin to feel.
At first, your conscience protests.
Then you explain.
Then you justify.
Then you repeat.
Eventually, what once broke your heart barely disturbs you.
That is one of the terrible effects of sin.
It does not always destroy a person's life with a loud explosion.
Sometimes it simply teaches them to become comfortable in a room where the lights have been turned off.
But John does not leave us there.
He brings us to one of the most beautiful promises in the New Testament.
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7 (KJV)
To understand what he means, we need to look closely at the original Greek.
The phrase translated “walk in the light” is:
ἐν τῷ φωτὶ περιπατῶμεν
en tō phōti peripatōmen
The verb περιπατῶμεν comes from περιπατέω (peripateō), meaning “to walk.”
In biblical usage, walking can describe the way someone conducts their life.
Here, the verb is in the present subjunctive within John's conditional statement.
John is not talking about physically walking through sunlight.
He is describing a way of life lived in relation to God's revealed truth and holiness.
To walk in the light is to live openly before God, responding to His truth rather than making darkness your home.
It includes honesty.
Repentance.
Obedience.
Fellowship.
A growing willingness to allow God's Word to expose what needs to change.
But here is where we must be extremely careful.
Walking in the light does not mean living a sinlessly perfect life.
If it did, John's next words would make no sense.
Because just two verses later, he writes:
Read that again.
John includes himself and his fellow believers in the discussion.
He does not say that Christians who walk in the light never need cleansing.
In fact, the promise of cleansing in verse 7 assumes that sin remains a serious reality that must be dealt with.
Walking in the light is not pretending you have no sin.
It is refusing to build your life around the lie that your sin does not matter.
It is coming into God's truth rather than hiding behind religious appearances.
And this distinction can change everything for someone who has been drowning in shame.
Because some people have been taught to believe that every failure means they have completely lost their place before God.
They sin.
They grieve.
They confess.
They try again.
Then they fall into despair because they assume that a genuine Christian would never struggle so deeply.
But the apostle John refuses both dangerous extremes.
He does not give permission to continue comfortably in sin.
And he does not demand that believers pretend they are already without sin.
He tells us to walk in the light.
Then he tells us what to do when the light reveals our sin.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
There is another Greek word worth understanding here.
ὁμολογῶμεν
homologōmen
It comes from ὁμολογέω (homologeō), meaning “to confess,” “to acknowledge,” or “to agree.”
In this passage, confession is not a performance designed to impress God.
It is an honest acknowledgment of sin before Him.
It is no longer calling evil good.
No longer renaming disobedience as harmless.
No longer pretending that what God has exposed does not exist.
It is the sinner finally saying:
“Lord, You are right about this. I have sinned. I cannot justify it. I need Your mercy.”
And look at what John says God does.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because our tears are powerful enough to wash away guilt.
Not because our promises to do better can erase what has already happened.
But because God is faithful and just, and the saving work of Jesus Christ is the righteous foundation of our forgiveness.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because the blood of Jesus is not a religious metaphor for positive thinking.
It points to His actual sacrificial death.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He loved people who could never earn His love.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He exposed darkness without becoming corrupted by it.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because He had sinned.
But because we had.
Peter writes:
Jesus did not die merely to make us feel less guilty.
He died to deal with the guilt and power of sin and to bring sinners back to God.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of our rebellion and the astonishing greatness of divine love.
Our sin was not insignificant.
If sin were harmless, the cross would be unnecessary.
But God's mercy was not insufficient.
If the cross of Christ were powerless, our hope would be empty.
And the resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ is alive.
That means the person who has been hiding does not have to remain hidden.
The one who has fallen does not have to call failure their permanent identity.
The one who has wandered does not have to conclude that the door of mercy has closed.
Listen carefully.
The blood of Jesus is not permission to love the darkness. It is the hope that allows us to leave it.
And perhaps you are wondering something right now.
“If walking in the light matters, does that mean I have to clean myself up before Jesus will forgive me?”
No.
Absolutely not.
That would reverse the Gospel.
We are not saved because we have successfully made ourselves righteous.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not mean that obedience becomes irrelevant.
It means obedience becomes the fruit of God's saving work rather than the price we pay to purchase salvation.
The order matters.
Jesus does not say, “Become clean enough, and then My blood will be available.”
The Gospel calls sinners to come to Christ in repentance and faith because only He can cleanse them.
And those who belong to Him are called to walk in the light of the One who has saved them.
Even our ability to grow in holiness depends upon His grace.
This is why John writes in the next chapter:
Do you see the tenderness?
“My little children…”
John is not speaking like someone who enjoys crushing wounded souls.
He writes with pastoral concern.
His purpose is that believers would not sin.
Yet he immediately reminds them that when they do sin, they have an Advocate with the Father.
Jesus Christ the righteous.
The Greek word translated “advocate” is παράκλητον (paraklēton), referring here to one who comes to another's aid or represents their cause.
Jesus is not an Advocate because the Father is reluctant to show mercy.
The Father Himself sent the Son in love.
Christ's advocacy rests upon who He is and what He has accomplished.
John continues:
“And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.” — 1 John 2:2 (KJV)
The Greek word is ἱλασμός (hilasmos).
It refers to Christ's atoning work in relation to sin, including the dealing with God's righteous judgment against sin.
Christ is not merely an inspiring example of sacrifice.
He is our atoning Savior.

And His saving work is sufficient beyond the boundaries of John's immediate community. The verse must not be turned into a claim that every person is automatically saved regardless of their response to Christ.
The New Testament consistently calls people to repent and believe the Gospel.
But no sinner should imagine that their particular history makes Jesus an inadequate Savior.
Think about that.
The person who knows exactly what they did.
The one who cannot forget the night everything went wrong.
The parent carrying guilt over words that wounded a child.
The husband or wife who betrayed trust.
The young believer trapped in a secret habit.
The churchgoer who has learned how to smile while their soul feels empty.
The person who walked away from God and is terrified of returning.
The Gospel does not tell these people to minimize their sins.
It tells them that Jesus Christ is greater than the sin they must honestly bring before Him.
And sometimes that is precisely what makes grace so difficult to receive.
We understand punishment.
We understand consequences.
We understand why people would reject us after learning the truth.
But mercy?
Mercy that does not pretend the sin was small?
Mercy that calls us to repentance and still offers forgiveness?
Mercy purchased through the suffering of the innocent Son of God?
That kind of grace confronts everything in us that wants either to justify ourselves or to condemn ourselves beyond hope.
And this brings us to a scene from the Gospel of Luke.
A woman enters a house where Jesus is dining.
She is known in the city as a sinner.
People have opinions about her.
Her reputation has arrived before she has even spoken.
And there she stands, weeping at the feet of Jesus.
Her tears fall.
She wipes His feet with her hair.
She kisses His feet.
She anoints them with ointment.
The religious host sees her and silently questions Jesus.
Surely, if Jesus knew what kind of woman she was, He would reject her.
But Jesus knows.
He knows her history.
He knows the judgment in the room.
He knows the thoughts of the man who considers himself morally superior.
And Jesus tells a story about two debtors whose debts are forgiven.
Then He speaks of the woman's love in connection with the forgiveness she has received.
Finally, He tells her:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.” — Luke 7:50 (KJV)
Do not miss the beauty.
Her tears did not purchase salvation.
Her public humiliation did not earn forgiveness.
Jesus identified faith as the means through which she received His saving mercy.
And the religious man who was so occupied with her scandal had failed to recognize the depth of grace standing before him.
How many of us still make that mistake?
We look at somebody else's visible failure and forget our own desperate need for mercy.
We compare sins.
We rank scandals.
We decide whose past is too ugly to belong in church.
But at the cross, human pride has nowhere to stand.
Every forgiven believer is a recipient of grace.
And every sinner who comes to Christ must come through the same Savior.
This does not erase earthly consequences.
A person who has harmed others may still need to confess wrongdoing, make restitution, accept accountability, or face appropriate legal consequences.
Forgiveness does not mean that trust is instantly restored.
Repentance does not require victims to ignore danger or remain in abusive situations.
Walking in the light means truth matters, including truth about the harm sin has caused.
But even there, God's grace calls us away from deception and toward genuine transformation.
And maybe that is where this article is meeting you.
Not in a dramatic scandal everyone knows about.
But in a quiet battle nobody sees.
Perhaps you have become very good at hiding.
You know how to answer, “I'm fine.”
You know how to post encouraging Scriptures while feeling spiritually distant.
You know how to pray in public while avoiding honest prayer in private.
You know how to keep your reputation intact while your conscience is begging for attention.
And you are tired.
So tired.
Not merely tired of being tempted.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of promising yourself that tomorrow will be different.
Tired of wondering whether God is still listening.
Please hear what Scripture actually says.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The promise is not that you are powerful enough to repair your soul.
The promise is that God is faithful.
The promise is that Christ's atoning work is sufficient.
The promise is that sin does not have to be hidden behind an invented version of yourself.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent.
You can seek help.
You can begin making the difficult decisions that genuine repentance requires.
You can stop protecting the very thing that is destroying your peace.
And you can do all of this while depending on Jesus, not pretending you can save yourself.
There is something else in 1 John 1:7 that we often overlook.
John does not only speak about cleansing.
He also says:
“We have fellowship one with another.”
Walking in the light is not merely a private spiritual experience.
It has implications for how believers live together.
The word translated “fellowship” is κοινωνία (koinōnia), describing sharing or participation in a common relationship.
John has already spoken about fellowship with the Father and His Son Jesus Christ in 1 John 1:3.
Now he connects walking in the light with fellowship among believers.
That is significant.
Because darkness isolates.
Shame whispers, “Nobody can know.”
Pride insists, “You must handle this alone.”
Fear says, “If they knew the real you, they would never look at you the same way.”
And sometimes those fears have been strengthened by painful experiences with judgmental or unsafe people.
That pain should not be dismissed.
But Christian fellowship was never meant to be a theater where everybody performs perfection.
It is meant to be a community shaped by the truth and grace of Jesus Christ.
A place where sin is not celebrated, but repentant sinners are not treated as disposable.
A place where the wounded can receive care.
A place where accountability is practiced with humility.
A place where people pray for one another.
A place where those who fall are restored with gentleness, as Galatians 6:1 teaches.
This does not mean confessing every private struggle publicly or trusting everyone with sensitive details.
Wisdom matters.
Confidentiality matters.
Safety matters.
But hiding indefinitely from every trustworthy source of spiritual support can allow sin and shame to grow stronger.
Sometimes walking in the light means speaking honestly with a mature believer, pastor, counselor, or another appropriate person who can help you take responsible steps toward healing and obedience.
Sometimes it means deleting the hidden account.
Ending the deceptive relationship.
Returning what was stolen.
Telling the truth you have been avoiding.
Asking forgiveness without demanding that the injured person immediately trust you again.
Sometimes it means admitting, “I need help.”

And sometimes it means recognizing that your spiritual struggle has become tangled with trauma, addiction, depression, or another serious difficulty that deserves qualified care alongside pastoral support.
None of these steps earns salvation.
But grace does not teach us to protect the darkness.
It teaches us to walk toward the light.
And here is something that may surprise you.
The light that exposes your sin is not the enemy of your soul.
God's truth may make you uncomfortable.
It may interrupt your plans.
It may reveal a pattern you have spent years defending.
It may confront the version of Christianity you have constructed to avoid surrender.
But exposure is not always destruction.
In the hands of a holy and merciful God, exposure can become the beginning of repentance.
Think of Peter.
He loved Jesus.
He made bold promises.
He insisted that he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
But when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing his Lord.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine the weight of that moment.
He had not merely made a mistake in judgment.
He had denied the very One he had promised never to abandon.
If Peter had written the final chapter of his own story that night, perhaps it would have ended with failure.
But Jesus was not finished.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
The same Peter who had denied Him would later boldly proclaim the risen Christ.
This does not make denial insignificant.
It makes restoration astonishing.
Peter's failure was real.
His tears were real.
His restoration was real.
And the risen Jesus was greater than Peter's worst moment.
That is what makes the Gospel different from the empty reassurance that says, “Your sins don't matter.”
They matter deeply.
So deeply that Jesus went to the cross.
But they are not greater than the Savior who died and rose again.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to stop defining their entire life by the worst thing they have ever done.
You are responsible for your choices.
You may need to face consequences.
You may have difficult work ahead in making things right.
But if you are turning to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, your failure does not have the authority to overrule His Gospel.
He is not asking you to invent an innocent past.
He is calling you into a redeemed future.
It is a declaration of what Christ can do in a human life.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing the pain that others may have suffered.
But by bringing the truth into the light, granting forgiveness through His blood, and beginning a transformation that reaches far deeper than reputation.
Jesus rewrites everything not because He changes history into fiction, but because He changes the sinner's relationship to God and gives a new direction to the life that follows.
The past may still be remembered.
The scars may still be visible.
Some consequences may remain.
But shame no longer needs to be the master of the person who belongs to Christ.
And sin no longer needs to be defended as though it were a friend.
Now return to the words that started this entire conversation.
“The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.”
The Greek expression translated “cleanseth us” is:
καθαρίζει ἡμᾶς
katharizei hēmas
The verb καθαρίζει (katharizei) comes from καθαρίζω (katharizō), meaning “to cleanse” or “to purify.”
It is a present-tense verb.
In this context, it describes the cleansing work of Christ's blood in the life of those walking in the light.
Some interpreters emphasize the ongoing significance of this present tense.
That is consistent with John's concern for believers who continue to need forgiveness and cleansing.
But we should not exaggerate what Greek grammar alone proves.
The present tense does not mean Jesus is repeatedly sacrificed.
Hebrews 10:10–14 teaches that Christ offered Himself once for all, and that His single sacrifice is sufficient.
The continuing application of cleansing rests on that completed sacrifice.
Jesus does not need another cross.
His sacrifice is enough.
And the phrase “from all sin” is equally important.
The Greek is:
ἀπὸ πάσης ἁμαρτίας
apo pasēs hamartias
Literally, “from every sin” or “from all sin.”
The scope of the cleansing is extraordinary.
John does not identify a special category of sin that is too dirty for Christ's blood to cleanse.
He does not tell the repentant believer that some past failures must remain spiritually unforgiven because they were especially shameful.
The promise is comprehensive.
Yet we must not separate it from the surrounding verses and turn it into permission for deliberate unbelief or unrepentant rebellion.
The same passage that celebrates cleansing also condemns lying about our fellowship with God and denying the reality of sin.
And later, John makes clear that genuine knowledge of Christ cannot be separated from obedience to His commandments.
The Bible's message is not that sin is harmless because grace exists.
It is that grace is powerful enough to forgive sinners and begin changing their lives.
The blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.
And the Jesus whose blood cleanses us calls us to walk in the light.
These truths belong together.
Not in competition.
Not as opposites.
But as parts of one glorious Gospel.
So let me ask you something.
Not as someone standing above you.
Not as someone pretending to have never needed mercy.
But as one human being speaking to another who will one day stand before God.
What are you still hiding?
What have you been excusing because nobody has confronted you?
What have you convinced yourself is harmless, even though Scripture has already shown you otherwise?
What wound are you covering with a smile instead of bringing it honestly before the Lord?
What confession have you postponed?
What act of obedience have you delayed?
What relationship, habit, ambition, resentment, or secret compromise has slowly taken a place in your heart that belongs to Christ?
You do not need to answer those questions publicly.
You do need to take them seriously before God.
Because the most dangerous darkness is not always the darkness we can recognize.
Sometimes it is the darkness we have learned to defend.
And there is no freedom in spending your entire life protecting a lie.
If this message has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past that conviction.
Open your Bible.
Read 1 John 1:5–2:2 for yourself.
Pray honestly.
Confess what God has revealed.
Turn away from the sin you have been protecting.
Trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
And if you need help taking practical steps, seek wise and trustworthy support.
You do not have to publish your private struggles to prove that your repentance is genuine.
But you can stop pretending before God.
Maybe tonight your prayer will not sound impressive.
Maybe you will not have eloquent words.
Maybe all you can manage is:
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I have sinned.”
“I am tired of pretending.”
“I cannot save myself.”
“Please forgive me. Teach me to walk in Your light.”
That is not a magic formula.
It is simply the kind of honest dependence upon Christ that the Gospel calls us toward.
And if you belong to Him, do not confuse the grief of repentance with the hopelessness of condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The answer to your sin is not to run farther from Christ.
It is to come to Him in truth.
Because the cross is not where God pretended sin did not exist.
It is where the Son of God bore sin so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
And that is why this message must not end with fear.
It must end with Jesus.
The One who is the light of the world.
The One who loved sinners without approving their sin.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who shed His blood.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who calls people to repent and believe.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who is worthy of every part of our lives.
Not just our Sunday mornings.
Not just our worship songs.
Not just the public version of ourselves.
Every part.
Even the hidden places.
Especially the places we have been afraid to surrender.
And perhaps this is where your story begins to change.
Not because you have finally become strong enough.
But because you have stopped treating darkness as your refuge and have begun trusting the Savior who is the light.
If these words reached you at a moment when your faith feels exhausted, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not owe strangers the details of your private battles.
But your honest words may encourage another believer who thought they were the only one still fighting.
Not to glorify your past, but to magnify the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Someone may need to hear that grace is not just a doctrine written on a page.
It is the truth of a living Savior who still transforms lives.
And please, do not allow this message to stop with you.
Not merely because it is emotionally moving.
Someone who would never walk into a church to ask for help might still read a Gospel-centered message that appears in their feed.
Someone who has been hiding behind a smile might finally open their Bible again.
Someone who has misunderstood grace as permission to continue in sin might discover the beauty of repentance.
Someone who has believed that their sin is too great for forgiveness might encounter the promise of Christ's cleansing blood.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still searching for answers about God to follow along.
We are not here to build a religion of appearances.
We want to keep pointing people to the living Christ.
And if these messages have helped you grow in your faith, I also want to invite you into something deeper.

The mission of Gospel Warrior is to continue sharing Scripture, producing Christ-centered teaching, encouraging struggling believers, reaching people who have not yet understood the Gospel, and creating resources that help Christians grow in biblical truth.
This work requires time, effort, and resources.
You are voluntarily helping sustain and expand a ministry effort devoted to proclaiming Jesus Christ.
For believers who wish to give in this way, it can be part of their broader stewardship before God.
What makes Christian giving beautiful is not pressure.
It is love.
It is gratitude.
It is the desire to use what God has entrusted to us for purposes that honor Him.
These resources are not what make the Gospel powerful.
Jesus does.
They are simply practical ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and help sustain the work.
And there is more.
Because the Gospel must never become something people can only hear if they pay.
Salvation is the gift of God.
The truth of Scripture is not for sale.
There is no need to give beyond your means or act out of guilt.
It is about Christ being proclaimed.
It is about Scripture being understood.
It is about sinners hearing the call to repentance.
It is about weary believers being reminded of the grace that sustains them.
It is about families opening the Word of God together.
It is about people discovering that their darkest chapter does not have to be their final chapter when they turn to Jesus Christ.
And if even one person who has been running from God hears the Gospel, repents, and places their trust in Jesus, that is reason to rejoice.
Before you leave, I want you to remember the verse that brought us here.
“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.”
Do not separate the light from the blood.
Do not turn grace into an excuse for darkness.
Do not turn holiness into an attempt to earn salvation.
Do not turn your failures into a verdict that Christ Himself has not pronounced.
Come to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Believe His Gospel.
Walk in His light.
When you stumble, do not defend your sin. Return to the Savior.
When you are convicted, do not silence the truth. Respond in repentance.
When you are forgiven, do not boast in yourself. Glorify the One whose blood has cleansed you.
And when you see another struggling sinner turning toward Christ, remember how much mercy you yourself have received.
There is no greater Savior.
No more sufficient sacrifice.
No more glorious hope.
Because Jesus Christ does not merely make guilty people feel better about their darkness.
He calls them out of it.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
And one day, all who belong to Him will see Him as He is.
Until then, keep walking in the light.
Not to make Jesus love you.
But because in Christ, you have encountered a love too holy to leave you unchanged.
The darkest chapter of your life does not have to be the final word—because the blood of Jesus can cleanse what shame could never erase.
